docs.title: patch-order-bench
docs.text:
A benchmark for the order a patch programme works in. It takes a vulnerability backlog, spends a fixed remediation capacity against it under eight different orderings, and scores what each one bought.

The question it exists to answer: a scanner sorts by CVSS descending, and CVSS measures how bad a vulnerability would be if exploited, not whether anyone is exploiting it. How much does that cost?

docs.title: Read this first
docs.text:
Every number published here is a simulation of

5,000 generated findings, not a measurement of a real estate. The live feed path reads EPSS and the CISA KEV catalogue, has tests against recorded responses, and has never been run against the real endpoints.

  • Sources separates the one parameter with published provenance from the choices.
  • Limitations is the list of reasons not to over read these figures, and it is longer than the results page.

docs.title: The result in one picture
docs.text:
No ordering wins on both axes. Putting the known exploited findings first covers

1.000 of them and attains

0.084 of the reachable compliance windows. Working the windows attains

0.649 and covers

0.202 of the exploited findings. A programme is choosing between these whether or not it knows it is.

The full table, every spread, and the sensitivity sweep are on the results page.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install patch-order-bench

pob columns findings.csv                      # see what your exporter called things
pob compare --csv findings.csv --map map.json # score all eight orderings

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• ADR 001: rank by exploitation probability, not severity, and what the measurement actually supports.
  • ADR 002: no persistence layer, and an argument the dependency checker falsified.
  • ADR 003: how the simulation earns the right to a number, including the striking result that turned out to be noise.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Read this before quoting any number from this project.

docs.title: It is a simulation, end to end
docs.text:
No figure here was measured against a real vulnerability backlog. The corpus is generated, the remediation programme is a model of capacity spent per week, and the live feed path has never run against the real feeds. docs/sources.md lists the single distributional parameter that has published provenance; everything else is a declared choice.

What this project can legitimately claim is that under a stated and swept set of assumptions, these orderings produce these outcomes, and that the code producing that claim is in the repository and reruns in under a minute. It cannot claim that a real programme would see these numbers.

docs.title: The headline metric is partly a tautology
docs.text:
KEV coverage measures what share of the known exploited findings got remediated, and the winning orderings are the ones that sort by the KEV flag. Of course they win. A benchmark where the metric is the sort key is measuring its own definition.

This is why the comparison is not reported on KEV coverage alone. Window attainment and exposure removed are scored in the same table, no ordering leads on all three, and the orderings that dominate KEV coverage are near the bottom on windows: kev-then-epss attains

0.084 against window-first at

0.649. The useful finding is the tension, not the win.

The one place KEV coverage is informative on its own is effort: kev-then-epss reaches 90 percent of the known exploited findings after

121 remediations out of a budget of

1,040, which says the catalogue is small enough to clear early rather than that sorting by it works.

docs.title: Twelve seeds is not many
docs.text:
The spread column in docs/results.md is the range across

12 seeds, and for the severity ordering it is 0.645, which is wider than most of the differences the table reports. Twelve seeds gives a mean with real uncertainty around it, not a settled figure.

The practical consequence: the orderings that score 1.000 with a spread of 0.000 are robust, and the ones in the middle of the table should not be ranked against each other on these runs. Raise --seeds before drawing a conclusion from a small gap. The project publishes the spread rather than a confidence interval because a parametric interval on twelve samples of an unknown distribution would be more precise looking and no more honest.

docs.title: The corpus generator is not a model of a real backlog
docs.text:
It produces findings whose EPSS distribution is fitted to one published share and whose severity correlates with exploitation probability at a chosen strength. Real backlogs have structure this does not reproduce: findings cluster by asset and by software component, so remediating one often remediates many; ages are not uniform; scanner duplicates and false positives consume capacity; and exploitation probability is not independent across a fleet running the same stack.

The clustering omission matters most, and it cuts against this project's own conclusion. If one patch clears forty findings, an ordering that groups by component may beat any ordering that ranks findings individually, and no ordering in this tool groups by component.

docs.title: Capacity is modelled as a single fungible number
docs.text: One remediation is one unit of effort. In practice a kernel upgrade on a database cluster and a browser update are not the same unit, change windows are not evenly spaced, and some remediations are blocked on a vendor rather than on capacity. A model where effort is fungible flatters every ordering equally, so it probably does not change the ranking, but it does make the absolute attainment figures optimistic.

docs.title: EPSS is a thirty day probability and the simulation is not
docs.text: EPSS predicts exploitation in the next thirty days. This simulation spends capacity over 26 weeks and scores a single EPSS value per CVE throughout, as though the probability were static. Real EPSS scores move, sometimes sharply, when exploitation is observed. A programme rereading the feed weekly would reorder its backlog as it went, which is strictly more information than any ordering here uses.

docs.title: There is no notion of risk accepted or compensating controls
docs.text: Every finding in the corpus is remediable and worth remediating. Real programmes carry findings behind a WAF rule, on a segmented network, or formally risk accepted, and those are not failures of prioritisation.

docs.title: What would make this stronger
docs.text:
In roughly descending order of how much it would change the conclusions:

  1. Run it against a real anonymised backlog, even one.
  2. Add component clustering to the generator, and a grouping ordering to compete.
  3. Replay historical EPSS and KEV snapshots so the scores move during the simulation instead of standing still.
  4. Model effort as a distribution rather than a unit.
  5. More seeds.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Generated by tools/generate_results_doc.py from docs/metrics.json. Reproduce with make bench.

docs.title: Every figure here is a simulation
docs.text: Every figure in this file is a simulation. The live feed path in pob.feeds has never been run against the real feeds, because the environment this was built in cannot reach epss.cyentia.com or cisa.gov. One distributional parameter is sourced, from FIRST's EPSS model documentation: 3,735 of 139,473 CVSS 3.x CVEs score at or above 0.1. Every other parameter is a declared choice, and the one everything depends on, the correlation between severity and exploitation probability, is swept in experiment B rather than argued for.

docs.title: The corpus
docs.text:
5,000 findings over about 852 CVEs, 134 of them known exploited, averaged over 12 seeds. 3,248 findings were already past their PCI window on day one, which is what a real backlog looks like and is why window attainment has a ceiling.

The realized rank correlation between severity and exploitation probability came out at 0.225, and the realized share of CVEs at or above EPSS 0.1 at 0.0235 against a sourced target of 0.0268. Both are reported because they are what the measurement ran on, rather than what was asked for.

docs.title: The comparison
docs.text:
A programme doing 40 remediations a week for 26 weeks, which is 1,040 in total against a backlog of 5,000. Capacity has to bind, or there is nothing to prioritise.

At this rate the most window compliance any ordering could achieve is 170 findings, and the attainment column is a share of that rather than of the backlog.

ordering KEV coverage spread over seeds effort to 90% of KEV window attainment exposure removed cvss 0.382 0.645 never reached 0.132 0.347 epss 1.000 0.000 274 0.075 0.939 kev-then-epss 1.000 0.000 121 0.084 0.939 kev-then-cvss 1.000 0.000 121 0.107 0.657 exposure 0.991 0.056 384 0.059 0.949 due-date 0.212 0.357 never reached 0.000 0.222 window-first 0.202 0.446 never reached 0.649 0.172 random 0.211 0.108 never reached 0.064 0.219

No ordering wins on both axes, and that is the result. epss covers the known exploited findings best; window-first meets the most compliance windows; neither is second at the other's job. A programme has to choose which it is optimising, and most choose neither on purpose, because they rank by whatever the scanner printed.

Ranking by severity covers 0.382 of the known exploited findings against a shuffled backlog's 0.211. It is better than no ordering, and it is a long way behind putting the catalogue first.

docs.title: How much to trust these
docs.text: The spread column is the range across 12 seeds, and for cvss it is 0.645, which is wider than most of the differences in the table. A single run can land almost anywhere inside that, which is why the benchmark averages and why a reader wanting a tighter figure should raise the seed count rather than quote one of these to three decimal places.

docs.title: Does the conclusion survive its own assumption
docs.text:
The correlation between severity and exploitation probability is the parameter nothing in this project knows and everything depends on: at a correlation of 1 the two orderings are the same ordering. So it is swept rather than argued for.

correlation realized severity ordering KEV first shuffle verdict 0.00 -0.027 0.268 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins 0.20 0.162 0.368 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins 0.40 0.354 0.485 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins 0.60 0.555 0.741 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins 0.80 0.768 0.936 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins 1.00 1.000 0.997 1.000 0.190 exploitation ordering wins

The conclusion holds across the range. It never flips, and at the top of the range the two converge, which is what should happen if the mechanism is the one claimed: at a perfect correlation the severity ordering and the exploitation ordering are the same ordering.

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
findings generate slowest ordering seconds 5,000 0.05s window-first 0.014s 50,000 0.57s window-first 0.222s 500,000 7.57s window-first 2.884s

Ranking and scheduling 500,000 findings takes 2.9 seconds for the slowest ordering. A ranking a programme cannot rerun weekly is a ranking it will stop rerunning.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: What this project took from outside itself, and what it made up. The distinction matters more here than in most repositories, because every published figure is a simulation and a reader has to be able to tell which inputs have provenance.

docs.title: The one sourced distributional parameter
docs.text:
FIRST, EPSS model documentation. https://www.first.org/epss/model

Of 139,473 CVEs with a CVSS 3.x score, 3,735 score at or above an EPSS of 0.1, which is 0.0268. That share is the single anchor the generated EPSS distribution is fitted to. It is the only distributional parameter in this project that came from a published measurement rather than from a choice, and CorpusSpec.describe() prints it in a group of its own for that reason.

Everything else about the generated corpus, including the correlation between severity and exploitation probability that the whole comparison rests on, is a declared choice. The correlation is swept rather than defended. See docs/adr/adr-003-simulation-methodology.md.

docs.title: Definitions the tool has to get right
docs.text:
EPSS, Exploit Prediction Scoring System. FIRST. https://www.first.org/epss/model

A probability, between 0 and 1, that a CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next thirty days. It is a prediction with a time horizon, not a severity measure and not a statement about impact. Ordering a backlog by EPSS answers "what is most likely to be attacked soon" and does not answer "what would hurt most if it were". The tool keeps the two signals in separate fields on Vulnerability so that nothing in the codebase can quietly treat one as the other.

CVSS v3.1 specification. FIRST. https://www.first.org/cvss/v3.1/specification-document

Base score and the qualitative severity bands used by severity_from_cvss: none at 0.0, low from 0.1, medium from 4.0, high from 7.0, critical from 9.0. The base score measures intrinsic severity assuming exploitation, which is why this project treats it as an impact proxy rather than as a likelihood.

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. Established by Binding Operational Directive 22-01. https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog

A list of CVEs with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. It is an observation rather than a prediction, which is why the orderings that put it first are the ones that win on KEV coverage: the catalogue is the ground truth the metric is scored against. That is a tautology in the benchmark and a real advantage in practice, and docs/limitations.md says so rather than letting the result stand unqualified.

PCI DSS v4.0, requirements 6.3.1 and 6.3.3. PCI Security Standards Council. https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/

6.3.1 is the risk ranking process. 6.3.3 requires that critical or high security patches, identified by that process, are installed within one month of release, and that all other applicable security patches are installed "within an appropriate time frame as determined by the entity", with three months given as an example.

The remediation windows in pob.models are 30 days for critical and high, and 90 days for the rest. The 30 is the standard's requirement. The 90 is the standard's example, adopted here as this project's choice, and a programme that has determined a different appropriate time frame is not out of compliance with 6.3.3 and is simply measuring against a different window than this benchmark does. Nothing in the tool treats 90 days as a mandate.

docs.title: Feeds the tool can read and this environment could not reach
docs.text:
pob fetch reads the live EPSS and KEV feeds:

  • EPSS scores: https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss
  • KEV catalogue: https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json

That code path has tests against recorded responses and has never been run against the real endpoints, because the network in the environment this was built in refuses them. It is written, it is typed, it sends a descriptive user agent, and it is unproven. Anyone with network access can prove or disprove it in one command, and the README says which command.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Abramowitz and Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions, formula 7.1.26. The rational approximation to the error function used by the vectorised normal CDF in pob.corpus.generate. The first version of that code called math.erf through np.vectorize, which is a Python loop wearing a NumPy costume.

Moore and Hodgson, and earliest deadline first scheduling. The attainability ceiling in pob.simulate.metrics is a greedy earliest deadline first pass over the findings whose deadlines are still reachable at the given capacity. EDF is optimal for minimising lateness only on a feasible set, which is why the pass filters to reachable deadlines first; running it on the open set returned a ceiling of zero and took two attempts to get right.

Spearman rank correlation. Used rather than Pearson wherever severity is compared against exploitation probability, because the EPSS fit is a monotone transform of a latent normal and Pearson on the transformed values measures the transform as much as the relationship.

docs.title: ADR 001: rank by exploitation probability, not by severity
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A remediation programme has a backlog larger than its capacity and has to pick an order. The default order is whatever the scanner printed, which is CVSS base score descending. CVSS base score is a severity measure: it answers how bad this would be if it were exploited. It does not answer whether anyone is exploiting it.

Two other signals answer closer to that question. EPSS is a model output, a probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next thirty days. CISA KEV is a catalogue of CVEs with observed exploitation, so it is an observation rather than a prediction, and it is small: a few thousand entries against hundreds of thousands of CVEs.

The claim that exploitation signal beats severity for ordering a backlog is widely repeated and rarely measured in a form a reader can rerun. This project exists to measure it, which means the decision recorded here had to be made after the measurement rather than before it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Rank by exploitation signal. Specifically, put the known exploited findings first and order the remainder by exploitation probability, which is the kev-then-epss ordering.

Keep severity as a tie breaker and as a second axis, not as the primary key.

Keep all eight orderings in the tool, including the ones that lose, because an ordering a reader cannot reproduce losing is an ordering they have to take on trust.

docs.title: What the measurement actually said
docs.text:
Against a simulated backlog of

5,000 findings and a programme doing 40 remediations a week for 26 weeks:

  • kev-then-epss covers

1.000 of the known exploited findings, and reaches 90 percent of them after

121 remediations. - cvss covers

0.382, and never reaches 90 percent inside the budget on any of the twelve seeds. - A shuffled backlog covers

0.211.

So the decision is supported, and the honest version of the result is narrower than the slogan. Three things qualify it.

The severity ordering is better than nothing, and the margin is noisy. It beats a shuffle on the mean, and its spread across seeds is

0.645, which is wider than the gap it wins by. One run of this benchmark can show severity ordering beating the shuffle comfortably or losing to it. See ADR 003 for how close this project came to publishing the losing run as a headline.

No ordering wins on both axes. Exploitation ordering reaches

0.084 window attainment, while window-first reaches

0.649 and covers only

0.202 of the known exploited findings. A programme under PCI DSS v4.0 6.3.3 has a compliance obligation measured in windows, not in exploitation. This benchmark does not tell that programme to ignore its obligation; it tells it that the two goals are in tension and that it is choosing between them whether or not it says so out loud.

Sorting by due date is the worst of both. It attains

0.000 of the window ceiling, because

3,248 findings are already past their window on day one, and an ascending sort by due date spends the entire budget on findings whose deadline cannot be met any more. The intuitive compliance ordering achieves no compliance at all. window-first, which skips the unreachable deadlines and takes the ones still in reach, is the ordering that actually serves the obligation.

docs.title: The part this cannot tell you
docs.text:
EPSS is a thirty day probability. Ordering by it is correct for the question "what is most likely to be attacked soon" and wrong for "what would hurt most". A system whose compromise ends the company is not deprioritised because its EPSS is low; it is deprioritised by this ordering, which is a reason to carry asset exposure as a separate input rather than to delete the severity signal. The exposure ordering in the tool is the crude version of that idea and scores

0.949 on exposure removed, the highest of the eight.

The correlation between severity and exploitation probability is the parameter this whole comparison rests on, and nothing here knows its real value. It is swept rather than assumed. See ADR 003 and docs/results.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The tool ships with a default ordering that has a measurement behind it and a named weakness.
  • Anyone disagreeing with the default can rerun the comparison with their own CSV through pob columns and pob rank, which is the point.
  • The multi-objective result has to be stated every time the headline is, or the headline is a half truth.

docs.title: ADR 002: no persistence layer
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The plan for this project included a Parquet cache for generated corpora. Corpus generation is the single most expensive step in the pipeline: at 500,000 findings it takes 7.57 seconds against

2.88 for the slowest of the eight orderings. The benchmark regenerates a corpus once per seed per experiment, and pandas and pyarrow were already declared as dependencies. Caching looked free, and it looked like it would pay for itself on the slowest thing here.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Do not build it. Corpora are either reproducible from a seed or already on disk as the user's CSV. There is nothing to persist that is not cheaper to recompute than to invalidate.

docs.title: Why the obvious optimisation is the wrong one here
docs.text:
A cache is correct when recomputation is expensive and the inputs are stable. Here the opposite holds on both counts.

Recomputation is cheap, and the cache key is not. A corpus is a pure function of CorpusSpec plus a seed. The spec has fourteen fields, several of them floats. A correct cache key is a hash of all of them, and every future field added to the spec is a field somebody has to remember to put in the key. Forget one and the cache returns a corpus generated under different assumptions, silently, and every number downstream is wrong in a way no test catches, because the test and the stale entry agree with each other. The failure mode of the cache is worse than the cost it removes.

The cache would never hit. This is the one that settles it. Generation is expensive, but the benchmark never generates the same corpus twice: each seed is a different corpus by definition, and each point in the sensitivity sweep is a different spec. A cache whose keys are all distinct is a write only cache. It would pay the cost of serialising every corpus to disk, in exchange for a hit rate of zero, and would leave behind a directory of large files nobody reads.

At the scale the published results actually run, 5,000 findings, generation takes

0.051 seconds. The argument for caching was built on the 500,000 finding row of a scaling table that exists to show the tool does not fall over, not on the workload the benchmark runs.

The real input is a CSV the user already has. For the path that matters, a scanner export on disk, Parquet adds a conversion step and a second copy of the user's vulnerability data, which is a thing to secure and a thing to delete. Reading the CSV each time is slower and is nobody's bottleneck at the sizes a single scanner export reaches. pob.corpus.load reads it with the standard library's csv module.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• pob generate writes a CSV when asked to and otherwise holds the corpus in memory. There is no cache directory, no cache invalidation, and no state between runs.
  • Reproducibility comes from the seed, which is printed in every result and recorded in docs/metrics.json, rather than from a stored artefact.
  • pandas and pyarrow are no longer dependencies. They were declared when this project expected to use them and nothing ever imported them, which tools/check_dependencies.py reported the first time it ran against a complete tree. An earlier draft of this ADR asserted that pyarrow was kept deliberately for reading Parquet scanner exports; that was a tidy explanation for a leftover, and the check falsified it. Two unused transitive dependency trees left the install.
  • If corpus generation ever becomes the bottleneck, the fix is to make the generator faster, which is a change with no correctness surface, rather than to remember more fields in a cache key.

docs.title: Note on how this was recorded
docs.text: The planning document for this project said "Parquet over a database" as the persistence decision. No persistence layer was built, so recording that decision would have described a thing that does not exist in the repository. This ADR records the decision actually taken.

docs.title: ADR 003: how the simulation earns the right to a number
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every figure this project publishes is a simulation. The live feed path in pob.feeds exists, has tests against recorded responses, and has never been run against the real feeds, because the environment it was built in cannot reach epss.cyentia.com or cisa.gov. That is stated in docs/metrics.json, in the README, and here, because a simulated number presented as a measured one is the single most damaging thing a project like this can do.

A simulation of a backlog can produce any result its author wants by choosing parameters. The methodology below is the set of constraints that make the output worth reading, and each one was added because the undisciplined version of the measurement was wrong.

docs.title: Sourced and chosen parameters are labelled separately
docs.text:
CorpusSpec.describe() splits its parameters into three groups: sourced, chosen, and scale. Exactly one parameter is sourced, from FIRST's EPSS model documentation:

0.0268 of CVSS 3.x CVEs score at or above EPSS 0.1. Everything else is a declared choice. Printing them in separate groups stops a reader from inferring that the whole distribution came from somewhere.

The realized values are reported next to the targets, because a generator does not necessarily produce what it was asked for. The realized share at or above 0.1 came out at

0.0235 against the sourced 0.0268, and the realized rank correlation at

0.225 against a requested 0.25. Those are the numbers the comparison actually ran on.

docs.title: The parameter the conclusion depends on is swept, not argued for
docs.text:
The correlation between severity and exploitation probability is unknown and decides the whole comparison: at a correlation of 1, ranking by severity and ranking by exploitation probability are the same ranking. Experiment B sweeps it from 0.0 to 1.0 and reports the verdict at each point. The conclusion holds across the range and the two orderings converge at the top of it, which is what should happen if the mechanism is the one claimed. A sweep that produced the same verdict at every point including correlation 1.0 would be evidence of a bug, not of robustness.

Early on it did exactly that, because the verdict function called a gap of 0.003 a win. It now requires a margin of 0.02 before calling either side ahead, and reports a tie otherwise.

docs.title: Results are averaged over seeds, and the spread is published
docs.text:
Twelve seeds, and the spread across them in the same table as the mean.

This is the rule that cost the project its best headline. A single seed showed the severity ordering covering 0.085 of the known exploited findings against a shuffled backlog's 0.211, which reads as "ranking by CVSS is worse than ranking at random", and which is the most quotable sentence this benchmark could have produced. Over twelve seeds it is

0.382 against

0.211. The striking version was noise. Its spread across seeds is

0.645, wide enough that single runs land almost anywhere, which is why the spread column exists and why twelve seeds is stated as a limitation rather than as sufficiency.

docs.title: Ceilings are capacity aware
docs.text:
Window attainment is reported as a share of what is reachable, not of the backlog.

3,248 findings are past their window on day one and no ordering can bring them back, and a programme with finite capacity cannot reach every remaining deadline either. The ceiling is computed by a greedy earliest deadline first pass over the findings whose deadlines are still reachable at the given capacity, which gives

170 findings.

The first version of this ignored capacity and reported a ceiling of 510, which understated every ordering's attainment by a factor of three. A denominator nobody can reach makes every ordering look equally bad, which conveniently flatters the comparison the project was making.

docs.title: Capacity holds its ratio to the backlog across scales
docs.text:
The sweep and the headline run at the same capacity share of the backlog. They did not at first, and a shuffled baseline that should have matched the headline's

0.211 came out at 0.54, because the sweep was giving the programme more capacity per finding. Two numbers in the same document that cannot both be right is the cheapest bug to find and the most expensive to publish.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The benchmark takes longer, because twelve seeds times six sweep points times eight orderings.
  • Every number in docs/results.md is generated from docs/metrics.json by tools/generate_results_doc.py, with --check in CI, so prose cannot drift from the measurement.
  • The limitations are a document rather than a sentence. See docs/limitations.md.
